summary: Real, dated trigger (EU PPWR applies since 12 Aug 2026; Etsy now asks for EPR IDs but tells sellers to work out the rules themselves), and a $29 plan is cheap against 190 EUR/country representatives. Demand for a plan (vs. having it done for them) is unproven, so it earns only a two-week waitlist test.

demand.evidence: No evidence anyone pays a third party for a plan. Evidence is pain and confusion: Etsy's petition post says sellers must determine requirements themselves; UK Business Forums and Etsy community threads show conflicting advice (400 EUR fee vs. 'file yourself'), though dated. Representatives at 190 EUR/yr and the EUReady app show adjacent spend. Interest, not demand.

statusQuo.evidence: Real workaround: free generic guides (Listadum), forum threads, paying a representative per country, or a spreadsheet. The cost of the status quo is concrete (570+ EUR/yr for 3 countries; fines up to 100k EUR DE, 30k EUR FR, vendor-sourced). Sellers are being asked for IDs by Etsy now, so inaction has a consequence.

specificity.evidence: Buyer is a category with a moment: non-EU Etsy/Shopify owner, $20k-$300k/yr, 2-6 EU countries, who just got the Etsy EPR prompt. No named person yet; reachable via Etsy seller forums and subreddits, but self-promotion risk.

wedge.evidence: Narrow and shippable: Germany and France (plus ES, IT) rules table with a pure buildPlan function, no accounts or DB. A free calculator lead magnet fits the test. The ledger, reminders and pay gate can wait.

futureFit.evidence: Rules churn helps a maintained source of truth, but an EU simplification, a platform pay-on-behalf scheme, or the Etsy petition could shrink the problem within a year. The Commission proposal to suspend the representative requirement is not adopted. Likely a 1-2 year window, not a durable business.

premises: Small non-EU sellers must act on EPR now: supported by PPWR timing and Etsy's ID collection, but enforcement against micro-sellers is unproven.
They want to understand and decide (which countries, what cost, whether to stop shipping) rather than have someone do it for them: unsupported; the research itself flags this as open.
A neutral $29 plan is worth paying for next to free guides: unproven; a free Listadum article covers much of the generic content.
A solo dev can keep the rules table accurate: plausible for 4 countries, a growing burden beyond that.
alternatives: Minimal: free per-country calculator and a one-page checklist with an email capture, monetised later by affiliate referral to a representative or scheme operator.
Ideal: the full packpass with questionnaire, rules table for 8 countries, ledger, reminders and Stripe paywall: more work and more maintenance before any demand proof.
Lateral: a paid, dated 'EU EPR rules digest' newsletter or Notion template for Etsy/Shopify sellers, with no app to run.
Extend an existing repo: feedwarden and permitly in David's portfolio share the 'rules change, alert the small operator' pattern, so the rules-table and diff scaffold can be reused.
wedge: A free Germany + France questionnaire that outputs an ordered checklist and a cost range for a US/UK Etsy self-shipper, with a $29 waitlist for the full multi-country plan and ID ledger.

feasibility.notes: Next.js on Vercel Hobby, rules.json in the repo, a pure buildPlan function, no database or accounts. One test proves M1: buildPlan with countries DE, FR, ES totals the sum of per-country mins, and every rules row has an https source plus an ISO verified date. The effort is in verifying the rules, not the code. A not-legal-advice disclaimer is required.

risks: Legal-advice liability and stale rows are a trust failure; every row needs a source and a last-verified date.
Vendor-sourced cost figures conflict, so show ranges only.
Buyers may want the registration done, not a plan; the plan alone may not convert.
EU simplification or platform pay-on-behalf could end the need within a year.
Distribution: seller forums are hostile to promotion, and the buyers are scattered.
Free guides and Etsy's own help capture much of the generic value.
killCriteria: Drop it if, after 14 days and about 200 targeted visitors, fewer than 10 sign up or click the $29 pre-pay (5%) and no one replies that they would pay; or if replies show sellers just stop shipping to the EU or only want a representative; or if the EU adopts the suspension or a platform takes over registration.

landing.headline: Etsy asked for your EU EPR number. Now what?
landing.subhead: Answer a few questions and get a country-by-country packaging registration plan with costs, labels and deadlines, for $29 instead of 190 EUR per country.
bullets: Which EU countries you must register in, and in what order
A cost range per country, and a flag when shipping there stops being worth it
Labels you need to print (e.g. Triman and Info-tri for France)
A ledger of your LUCID, IDU and representative IDs with filing reminders
landing.audience: Non-EU (US, UK, Canada, Australia) Etsy and Shopify shop owners who ship their own parcels to 2-6 EU countries.

launch.post: Etsy now asks for EPR numbers for France, Germany and Spain, but says sellers have to work out which rules apply. I'm trying to build a simple tool: you answer a few questions about where you ship and it gives you a checklist of what to register, roughly what it costs and what labels you need. It is information only, not legal advice, with sources. Early page: {url}. If you ship to the EU from outside it, what's the part you're most stuck on, and would you pay for a plan or would you rather have someone do the registration?
